Introduction

The combination of a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl is called a carboxyl group; carb- from carbonyl and –oxyl from hydroxyl. Compounds containing the carboxyl group are distinctly acidic and are called carboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids may be aliphatic or aromatic depending upon whether carboxyl group is attached to an alkyl group or an aryl group. The simplest acid is formic acid (HCOOH), with a hydrogen atom bonded to the carboxyl group, and also an aliphatic acid. Fatty acids are long-chain aliphatic carboxylic acids derived from the hydrolysis of fats and oils. Acids containing one such functional group are known as mono carboxylic acids, while those containing two carboxyl groups are called dicarboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids have many derivatives in which the –OH of an acid is replaced by other functional groups. Carboxylic acid derivatives are compounds with functional groups that can be converted to carboxylic acids by a simple acidic or basic hydrolysis. The most important acid derivatives are acid halides, esters, anhydrides, amides and nitriles.

Notice that in each case there is a carbon atom (highlighted in blue) with three bonds to heteroatoms. As a result, each of these carbon atoms has the same oxidation state as the carbon atom of a carboxylic acid. Thus, the inter-conversion of carboxylic acid and derivatives, do not involve change in oxidation state of this carbon. Although all of these derivatives (except nitrile) exhibit a carbonyl group, the presence of a carbonyl group is not a necessary requirement to qualify as a carboxylic acid derivative. Any compound with a carbon atom that has three bonds to heteroatoms that can be converted to carboxylic acids by a simple acidic or basic hydrolysis will be classified as a carboxylic acid derivative.

Introduction

The combination of a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl is called a carboxyl group; carb- from carbonyl and –oxyl from hydroxyl. Compounds containing the carboxyl group are distinctly acidic and are called carboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids may be aliphatic or aromatic depending upon whether carboxyl group is attached to an alkyl group or an aryl group. The simplest acid is formic acid (HCOOH), with a hydrogen atom bonded to the carboxyl group, and also an aliphatic acid. Fatty acids are long-chain aliphatic carboxylic acids derived from the hydrolysis of fats and oils. Acids containing one such functional group are known as mono carboxylic acids, while those containing two carboxyl groups are called dicarboxylic acids.

Carboxylic acids have many derivatives in which the –OH of an acid is replaced by other functional groups. Carboxylic acid derivatives are compounds with functional groups that can be converted to carboxylic acids by a simple acidic or basic hydrolysis. The most important acid derivatives are acid halides, esters, anhydrides, amides and nitriles.

Notice that in each case there is a carbon atom (highlighted in blue) with three bonds to heteroatoms. As a result, each of these carbon atoms has the same oxidation state as the carbon atom of a carboxylic acid. Thus, the inter-conversion of carboxylic acid and derivatives, do not involve change in oxidation state of this carbon. Although all of these derivatives (except nitrile) exhibit a carbonyl group, the presence of a carbonyl group is not a necessary requirement to qualify as a carboxylic acid derivative. Any compound with a carbon atom that has three bonds to heteroatoms that can be converted to carboxylic acids by a simple acidic or basic hydrolysis will be classified as a carboxylic acid derivative.

20.1 Nomenclature

Nomenclature of carboxylic acid

Following two types of naming is employed for naming of carboxylic acids.

(a) Common or Trivial Names
